papers.title: Expanding Plasma Proteome Coverage While Preserving Biological Signatures: A Systematic Characterization of Enrichment and Preanalytical Variables
papers.abstract: Plasma is a rich and accessible source for biomarkers. The analytical challenge of the steep dynamic range was recently addressed using enrichment technologies. Enrichment technologies have been shown to be sensitive to preanalytical variables, making this an active area of research. We established the P2 enrichment system as high-performing and robust for large scale studies, with reproducible identifications and precision across batches, days, operators and laboratories. We characterized P2-based enrichment for preanalytical variables (eight blood collection types, centrifugation, freeze-thaw and pathogen inactivation). K2EDTA-plasma resulted in the deepest proteome coverage with about 6000 protein groups on the timsTOF HT. We spiked 16 heavy-labelled proteins into platelet-poor and platelet-contaminated plasma. Importantly, linearity, accuracy, and precision were high in both platelet-poor and platelet-contaminated plasma for both P2-enriched and neat preparations. In a cancer cohort, we demonstrated that 97% of differentially abundant proteins retained the same direction of regulation after P2-based enrichment compared with the neat preparation. Differentially abundant proteins identified in a colorectal cancer pilot cohort remained largely conserved after platelet contamination, including previously reported biomarkers. We demonstrated that P2-based enrichment enables deep, large scale proteome profiling and preserves biological information despite preanalytical variation. Candidates emerging from P2-based discovery can be validated in independent cohorts with targeted assays.

papers.title: Intraspecific glucosinolate chemodiversity in Cardamine hirsuta
papers.abstract: Within some plant species, a high intraspecific chemical variation, termed chemodiversity, can be found in the composition of specialized metabolites. For Brassicales, glucosinolates are highly characteristic. Their composition is genetically determined but variation has been found within species and between organs in different species. Cardamine hirsuta is increasingly being used as genetic model species, but until now, little was known about its genetically-based variation in glucosinolates. Thus, we aimed to characterize glucosinolate profiles, their putative genetic variation and their chemodiversity in established accessions and wild-collected material. We analyzed the glucosinolate profiles of leaves and roots from offspring, grown under standardized conditions, of 18 accessions collected in nine countries. Glucosinolates were quantified by HPLC-DAD and identities were confirmed by UHPLC-QToF-MS/MS. Glucosinolate composition was analyzed in biosynthetic terms, compared across samples with principal component analysis and chemodiversity was quantified as glucosinolate richness and Shannon diversity. In total, 14 glucosinolates were confirmed across samples. Two main sources of variation among accessions were the relative levels of but-3-enyl- versus pent-4-enylglucosinolate and of benzylglucosinolate versus phenethylglucosinolate. An almost universal presence of 1-methoxyindol-3-ylmethylglucosinolate in roots but not leaves was observed, along with quantitative contrasts between leaves and roots. The glucosinolate composition varied profoundly among accessions and between leaves and roots, while offspring within accessions were mostly consistent in their profiles. Even accessions collected in close proximity produced distinct profiles, with no clear separation along latitude or longitude. Our study highlights two independent and chemically simple traits of apparently genetic nature, namely the extent of chain elongation of methionine-derived and of phenylalanine-derived glucosinolates. Their independent occurrence is a main factor shaping the glucosinolate profiles among accessions. High variation was also observed at a local scale, highlighting complex genetic variation in glucosinolate biosynthesis in the species throughout Europe. Moreover, within individuals different organs showed clearly distinct profiles, indicating organ-specific biosynthesis. The genetic basis and ecological consequences of this variation need to be explored in future studies.

papers.title: Actin Assembly on Biomimetic Lipid-coated and Functionalized Bead Surfaces
papers.abstract: Dynamic assembly of actin filaments drives cell protrusion and other aspects of cell motility. Reconstitution of actin assembly from purified components is a powerful approach for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie these processes. Purified preparations of actin, actin-binding proteins, and regulators of actin-binding proteins enable a broad spectrum of reconstitution experiments. Much of this actin filament assembly occurs at the plasma membrane, with exquisite temporal and spatial regulation. We developed a biomimetic reconstitution system using purified lipids or glutathione on the surface of functionalized beads as models for actin assembly at the plasma membrane. The system incorporates two critical pathways for regulation of actin assembly: nucleation of actin polymerization by Arp2/3 complex and activation of heterodimeric actin capping protein (CP). Arp2/3 complex and CP are both essentially inactive in the basal resting state of the cytoplasm. The system incorporates membrane-bound activators for Arp2/3 complex, such as WASP and WAVE family proteins, and for CP, such as CARMILs and other CPI-motif proteins. Membrane-bound components are coupled to beads either through lipids, which allow lateral mobility, or through glutathione groups attached to the bead surface via flexible linkers. Fluorescence microscopy of labeled components, combined with quantitative image analysis, is used to assess the combined effects of the regulators and thereby test molecular mechanisms for regulation of actin assembly. Here, we describe protocols for preparing functionalized beads, coupling regulators to the bead surface, performing actin assembly reactions, and imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.

papers.title: Proteomic Evaluation of the Progression from Acute Kidney Injury to Chronic Kidney Disease
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are interconnected syndromes with substantial global burden, yet the molecular mechanisms driving the transition from acute injury to chronic fibrosis remain incompletely understood. We performed quantitative data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) proteomics on mouse models of AKI (ischemia-reperfusion injury) and CKD (unilateral ureteral obstruction), quantifying 5,985 protein groups. A conserved core injury response of 1,475 shared proteins (46%) was dominated by mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of solute transporters, and immune and extracellular matrix remodeling. AKI was marked by chromatin reorganization, DNA damage response, and acute inflammation, whereas CKD showed sustained fibrosis, complement activation, and coagulation. Peroxisomal proteins, including the {beta}-oxidation enzymes Acox1 and Ehhadh, were consistently down-regulated in both AKI and CKD, with no peroxisomal protein up-regulated. Both models also displayed a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-like signature, including Havcr1, Spp1, Igfbp7, Plau, and lysosomal cathepsins. We further identified 95 candidate progression markers, including Brat1 and Col3a1, 93 proteins with greater loss in CKD, 14 proteins changing in opposite directions, and seven disease-associated co-expression modules. These findings provide a proteomics resource for biomarker discovery and therapeutic targeting, including peroxisomal restoration and senolytic strategies, in AKI and CKD.

papers.title: Lipid-Driven NRF2 Preconditioning Links Estrogen Deprivation to Hepatic Resilience Against Acetaminophen Injury
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: Menopause is associated with a sustained decline in estrogen signaling that profoundly alters hepatic lipid metabolism; however, its impact on the liver response to xenobiotic stress remains poorly understood. Given that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure (DILI) and that sex and age influence susceptibility to hepatotoxicity, we investigated how long-term estrogen deprivation affects the development of APAP-induced liver injury (AP-ILI). Methods: Clinical data from a multicenter cohort of patients admitted following APAP overdose were analyzed to assess susceptibility to AP-ILI. To model the postmenopausal state, 12-week-old female C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice underwent bilateral ovariectomy (OVX) or sham surgery and, six months later, were challenged with acetaminophen (360 or 600 mg/kg). Mechanistic studies included NRF2 silencing, estradiol replacement, and dietary lipid modulation using a high-fat diet. Comprehensive lipidomic profiling was performed to characterize hepatic lipid remodeling, while human liver biopsies were analyzed to validate the expression of key molecular targets. Results: Women [≥]50 years of age showed a lower risk of severe AP-ILI, a phenotype recapitulated in OVX mice. Long-term estrogen deprivation induced hepatic lipid remodeling characterized by larger lipid droplets and enrichment in saturated neutral lipids, leading to sustained NRF2 activation. Enhancement of lipid remodeling with high-fat diet increased NRF2 signaling and hepatoprotection, whereas estradiol replacement reversed these effects. Consistent with these findings, women over 50 years of age exhibited increased hepatic expression of NRF2 and its target genes. Conclusions: Long-term estrogen deprivation confers protection against AP-ILI through extensive hepatic lipid remodeling, characterized by lipid droplet expansion and altered neutral lipid composition, which promotes sustained NRF2 activation.

papers.title: Proteome-wide reanalysis identifies coverage and error-rate limits on acquired lysines in cancer
papers.abstract: Missense mutation in cancer creates acquired lysines, residues present in tumor cells and absent from normal cells in the same patient. The class holds 295,411 sites across 20,365 genes and falls on driver hotspots more often than other substitutions (odds ratio 1.68). Yet re-searching 42 proteomic experiments with a mutation-aware database recovers the mutant peptide in 0.63% of 8,470 site-in-cell-line observations, because a new lysine is a new cleavage site and the peptide it creates runs 6 residues against 13 for the wild type. Reported error rates do not hold either. Burden-matched entrapment puts the realized false-discovery proportion at 4.70% before score filtering, against 1% reported. Measured by competitive activity-based protein profiling across four cell lines, ligandability reproduces at the site level, no compound descriptor tested predicts it, and structure predicts it poorly at AUC 0.617. Acquired lysines are structurally ordinary, so the barrier is detection rather than chemistry.

papers.title: Receptor dynamics and kinetic discrimination contribute to selectivity of β1-adrenoceptor antagonists
papers.abstract: Human {beta}1-adrenoceptor (h[beta]1AR)-selective antagonists are widely used to suppress cardiac adrenergic signalling in cardiovascular disease with limited but still clinically relevant inhibition of h[beta]2AR functions in airway and vascular smooth muscle. However, achieving strong subtype selectivity remains challenging because the orthosteric binding sites (OBS) of h[beta]1AR and h[beta]2AR are highly conserved. Here we studied the molecular mechanisms for three highly subtype selective h[beta]1AR antagonists, CGP20712A, NDD713 and NDD825. Three cryo-EM structures were therefore determined for each of the ligands bound to an inactive state of turkey t[beta]1AR in complex with an engineered nanobody fiducial (Nb60.5) to facilitate image processing. There were striking differences in how each antagonist bound to the receptor compared to what was observed in previous antagonist-bound t[beta]1AR and h[beta]2AR structures; these included non-canonical binding of the oxypropan-2-olamine (secondary amine and [beta]-hydroxyl) cores of CGP20712A and NDD825 and the opening of a cleft between transmembrane helices H4 and H5 adjacent to the OBS. Mutagenesis of residues in the extended OBS that differ between h[beta]1AR and h[beta]2AR only partially explained the subtype selectivity. Subsequent kinetic analyses showed that all three ligands associated more rapidly with h[beta]1AR than h[beta]2AR, whereas dissociation effects were ligand dependent. Reciprocal receptor chimeras identified the h[beta]1AR extracellular vestibule as a key factor for fast ligand association. MD simulations further revealed that the cleft opening between H4 and H5 where CGP20712A and NDD825 insert is energetically feasible in h[beta]1AR, but is energetically inaccessible in h[beta]2AR. Together, these results establish that h[beta]1AR selectivity for CGP20712A and NDD825 arises from coordinated effects of OBS recognition, the ligand-entry pathway and receptor dynamics.

papers.title: Divergent Proteomic Responses to Lead Exposure in House Sparrows (Passer domesticus)
papers.abstract: Chronic exposure to environmental contaminants can drive population decline but also exert selective pressure favouring adaptive molecular responses that mitigate toxicity. Australian lead (Pb) mining and smelting towns provide a natural experiment to study such contemporary adaptation in the house sparrow (Passer domesticus), an invasive commensal species that has persisted in heavily contaminated environments for over a century. The Broken Hill population is of particular interest as it has remained geographically isolated with limited gene flow, whereas the Port Pirie population is connected to surrounding regions. Here, we used data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry to compare the blood and liver proteomes of wild-caught sparrows from both towns and identify divergent molecular responses to lead. Lead exposure altered the mitochondrial proteome and disrupted RNA splicing in both populations, but the two towns diverged sharply in haem biosynthesis and protein quality control. We identified a mechanistic cascade in which lead inhibits ALAD, depleting intracellular haem, stabilising the transcriptional repressor BACH1, and suppressing globin expression. Broken Hill birds maintained ALAD abundance, upregulated proteasomal subunits (PSMC) and HSP70 family chaperones, and preserved significantly higher haemoglobin concentrations despite equivalent blood lead levels. Port Pirie birds exhibited ALAD collapse, BACH1 accumulation, and reliance on autophagy rather than active protein quality control. Liver proteomics confirmed tissue-level convergence of the haem pathway disruption. Together, these findings reveal that over a century of isolation under sustained lead exposure has shaped population-specific molecular strategies in Broken Hill sparrows, with enhanced proteostasis and preserved haem biosynthesis representing signatures of local adaptation.

papers.title: Chemical crosslinking enables profiling of endogenous cell surface galectin-3 interactions
papers.abstract: Galectin-3 is a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin that organizes glycoproteins into cell surface lattices (multivalent interaction networks) that regulate biology spanning immune function, fibrosis, heart disease, and cancer progression. Galectin-3 engages promiscuous but low-affinity glycan ligands, posing technical challenges for faithfully mapping the cell surface galectin-3 interactome. Here, we introduce Crosslinking-assisted Galectin Lattice Affinity Purification Mass Spectrometry (xGL-APMS), a facile and stringent proteome-scale approach that captures galectin-3 interactions natively at the cell surface, without the need for exogenous galectin-3, and is extendable to XL-MS. We identified 125 N-glycan branching-dependent surface galectin-3 interactors on Jurkat cells, validated interactions with six orthogonal approaches, and compared low and high-dose galectin-3 interactomes, revealing differences in both distribution and interactome composition. Finally, without exogenous or modified bait, we performed immediate crosslinking of endogenous galectin-3 to identify 69 galectin-3-associated proteins on primary mouse thymocytes. Together, these approaches provide a readily adoptable framework for measuring endogenous surface galectin-3 and profiling its interacting partners.

papers.title: Aging Remodels the Female Skeletal Muscle Proteome Toward Matrix, Chromatin and Lysosomal Programs that Track Loss of Physical Function
papers.abstract: Loss of skeletal muscle strength and mobility is among the most consequential features of human aging, yet the molecular programs that accompany this decline in women remain poorly understood. Here, we performed deep comprehensive data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomic profiling of vastus lateralis biopsies from 10 younger (24-30 years) and 10 older (70-84 years) healthy women enrolled through the NIH Common Fund Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet), with matched measurements of grip strength and gait speed. Of 2,391 quantified protein groups, 163 were significantly altered with age, and partial least squares-discriminant analysis completely separated the age groups (cross-validated AUC = 1.00). Older muscle showed increased extracellular matrix and vascular remodeling proteins (TIMP3, COL8A1, ELN, FBN1), nuclear, chromatin and RNA-binding proteins (HMGB1, HMGB2, histone H1.0, MATR3, NCL), and lysosomal and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-associated proteins (CTSZ, CTSD, PSAP), together with reduced glycolytic and energetic proteins (GAPDH, ENO3, PHKA1, CYCS). Age effects were robust to adjust for body mass index (BMI). Integrating differential abundance, multivariate importance and participant-level consistency, we defined a 24-protein skeletal muscle aging signature whose score separated all younger from all elderly women. Combining grip strength and gait speed into a combined function score, we found that 23 of the 24 signature proteins correlated with physical function (FDR < 0.05), and the signature score correlated strongly with function (r = -0.79). The senescence-associated alarmins HMGB1 and HMGB2 emerged as lead proteins: HMGB1 showed the strongest association with function (r = -0.86), and both remained associated after adjustment for age group. Together, these data define a senotype proteomic program in aging female skeletal muscle and a molecular signature of muscle function that, after validation, may serve as a readout for interventions that aim to preserve physical performance in elderly women.

papers.title: SUMOylation Regulates IRF2BP2 Nuclear Localization and Stability
papers.abstract: Interferon Regulatory Factor-2 Binding Protein 2 (IRF2BP2) is a transcriptional cofactor implicated in diverse biological processes. Although it functions primarily as a repressor, it can also activate gene expression. However, the mechanisms governing IRF2BP2 regulation remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that IRF2BP2 interacts with UBE2I, the SUMO E2 ligase, and undergoes multi-SUMOylation, which enhances its nuclear localization. We further show that IRF2BP2 nuclear import is importin-{beta}-dependent and requires the functional nuclear localization signal (NLS). IRF2BP2 preferentially accumulates in transcriptionally active euchromatin in both resting and S-phase cells, consistent with its role in transcriptional control. We further reveal that SUMOylation contributes to IRF2BP2 stability. Moreover, IRF2BP2 is also ubiquitinated, predominantly through K6-linked ubiquitin chains, a non-proteolytic modification that aligns with our observation that IRF2BP2 is not degraded by the proteasome. Together, these findings identify SUMOylation and non-proteolytic ubiquitination as key mechanisms regulating IRF2BP2, highlighting a novel SUMO1-NLS-importin-{beta}-dependent pathway that governs its localization.

papers.title: S-adenosylmethionine supply controls DNA methylation turnover in synovial sarcoma
papers.abstract: Background: Methionine is the nutrient source of the metabolite S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) used to methylate chromatin for regulation of gene expression. Disruptions to this metabolic supply, including nutritional deficiency of certain B vitamins, alter chromatin methylation and have been implicated in tumor growth. Objective: To define how cellular SAM supply controls DNA methylation dynamics and the disruption of oncogenic gene expression in synovial sarcoma. Methods: Cell line models of synovial sarcoma were treated with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor azacitidine or the small-molecule MAT2A inhibitor AG-270, which blocks SAM synthesis from methionine. Intracellular SAM concentrations were quantified by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Global DNA methylation rates were measured by stable isotope tracing with [2H3-methyl]-methionine. Genomic sites of altered DNA methylation were identified by EM-seq and the associated transcriptional changes measured by RNA-seq. Results: Inhibition of SAM synthesis reduced intracellular SAM concentration from 94 uM to 5.6 uM (p value < 0.0001) at 24 hours. This was associated with a 19% decrease (p value < 0.0001) in the global 5-methyldeoxycytosine turnover rate, while total DNA methylation levels were maintained. In contrast to the global DNA hypomethylation induced by azacitidine, SAM depletion resulted in a redistribution of DNA methylation with loss at 252 and gain at 206 genomic sites, and the transcriptional response to SAM depletion was not associated with changes in promoter methylation at the altered genes. Both azacitidine and SAM depletion activated mesenchymal genes, while suppressing cell cycle progression. Conclusions: Metabolic supply of SAM is a major regulator of DNA methylation turnover providing a mechanism by which nutritional or genetic disruptions to SAM metabolism can alter chromatin methylation and gene expression.

papers.title: Structure of human hephaestin reveals a homodimer anchored to the cell membrane
papers.abstract: Hephaestin (Heph) is a membrane-bound ferroxidase that oxidizes ferrous ion (Fe2+) exported by ferroportin (Fpn) to ferric ion (Fe3+), enabling iron loading onto transferrin for systemic delivery. Loss-of-function mutations in Heph cause iron accumulation in intestinal enterocytes and systemic iron deficiency in animal models, underscoring its role in iron export. Heph has a large extracellular domain anchored to the cell membrane by a single transmembrane helix. However, full-length Heph has not previously been purified, and our understanding of its structure and function remains incomplete. Here, we report the expression and purification of functional fulllength human Heph and determination of its structure by cryo-electron microscopy at an overall resolution of approximately 2.3 [A]. The structure reveals a stable homodimer with well-resolved extracellular domains. Although the transmembrane helices are less well resolved, their positions can be defined. The substrate-binding site is connected to an electronegative funnel that may facilitate Fe2+ capture. These findings establish the structural organization of full-length human Heph and provide structural constraints for understanding its interaction with Fpn.

papers.title: Differential properties of gp120 from HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B
papers.abstract: HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B differ substantially in their gp120 sequence. To determine whether these differences contribute to subtype-specific complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), rats were injected with gp120 from subtype A or B. Pulmonary artery (PA) remodeling was assessed after four weeks using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and the Vessel Morphometry Analysis tool by Autona (autona.org). Subtype A gp120 potently increased PA wall thickness and right ventricular hypertrophy. The CD4-binding region of subtype A lacks a stretch of 16 amino acids (V1 N-glycosylation site), and experiments showed stronger binding of subtype B to CD4. Subtype B gp120 contains an RGKV sequence, which resembles the RGKR sequence of the rabies virus glycoprotein G that binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Subtype A gp120 possesses a KDKK sequence instead. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both sites are surface-exposed. Although nAChR is expressed in PA cells and could potentially drive the pronounced effects of subtype A, MD simulations estimated that subtype B gp120 binds more strongly to nAChR. We also noted a single amino acid difference immediately preceding the REKR furin cleavage sequence: glutamate in subtype A versus glutamine in subtype B gp120. Simulations predicted that subtype A gp120 interacts more effectively with furin, and enzyme assays demonstrated that subtype A promotes a positive feedback loop more strongly than subtype B. Thus, HIV-1 gp120 subtype A is more potent in promoting PAH, and the mechanism may involve enhancing furin activity to elevate gp120 levels.

papers.title: Affordable 96-parallel SPPS: hardware and software add-on for automated liquid handling platforms
papers.abstract: ParSynt-P is a hardware and software add-on that converts a liquid-handling robot already available in a proteomics laboratory (Tecan Freedom EVO) into a parallel plate-format peptide synthesizer for generating libraries of candidate peptide standards for targeted blood plasma proteomics. The manifold is milled from polytetrafluoroethylene and has ports for an inert gas and a vacuum line; a standard commercially available 96-well filtration plate is secured to it with an airtight seal. The software layer generates robot worklists from a table of peptide sequences and controls switching of the N?/vacuum lines, including pulsed gas mixing. The system performs up to 96 syntheses per run, and coupling of one residue takes 94 min. Workability of this 96-well format was verified on three fully loaded plates. The uniformity of synthesis conversion across the plate was measured quantitatively using a characterized NAT/SIL standard pair. The add-on cost $351, while the synthesis cost is $0.23 per coupling and $1.14 per milligram of crude product, an order of magnitude below the market price of custom synthesis.

papers.title: De novo design of ligases for programmable site-specific protein ubiquitylation
papers.abstract: Protein ubiquitylation regulates numerous cellular processes, but difficulties in generating site-specifically ubiquitylated proteins limit our understanding of individual modification events. In cells, ubiquitylation is mediated by an E1-E2-E3 enzyme cascade, with substrate recognition largely determined by more than 600 human E3 ligases, making it challenging to redirect ubiquitin transfer to a chosen lysine. Here we use RFdiffusion3 to design ubiquitin ligases from scratch that use a cysteine-based catalytic triad to conjugate an activated ubiquitin donor to a selected lysine in a chosen target substrate. Of 48 tested designs, 35 ubiquitylated a model peptide, with the most active ligases achieving near-quantitative ubiquitin transfer. We next challenged the approach with the homotrimeric sliding clamp proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), whose ubiquitylation at lysine (K) 164 governs DNA damage tolerance while displaying 45 off-target lysines for ubiquitination. Screening of 48 designs delivered a site-selective ligase. Incorporation of a single activity-increasing substitution and coupling to E1-dependent donor activation resulted in 90% conversion from unactivated ubiquitin, delivering higher rates and superior selectivity compared to a natural promiscuous E2. Using this cascade, we transferred di-, tri- and tetraubiquitin chains of defined length to PCNA K164 through a native isopeptide bond. These results establish de novo enzyme design as a route towards programmable, site-specific protein ubiquitylation. That a single de novo designed protein can bind both an activated ubiquitin donor and a globular target, and use a proficient catalytic machinery to selectively transfer ubiquitin to one lysine among 45, illustrates the level of functional complexity now within reach of de novo enzyme design.

papers.title: Impacts of Environmental Nickel and Chromium Exposure on the Blood Proteome of House Sparrows (Passer domesticus) in New Caledonia
papers.abstract: New Caledonia holds some of the world's largest ultramafic mineral deposits, and nickel (Ni) smelting operations have created a gradient of Ni and chromium (Cr) contamination across the archipelago. Molecular impacts of Ni and Cr toxicity on wildlife remain largely unexplored. Here, we used the house sparrow (Passer domesticus) as a sentinel species to characterise the blood proteomic response to Ni and Cr exposure near the Doniambo smelter in Noumea. Blood was collected from 52 free-living sparrows across 18 sites classified by soil metal concentration. Plasma and blood cell pellet fractions were analysed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Plasma proteomics identified histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG) as the most prominent responder, with approximately 2.1-fold elevation in exposed relative to low-exposure birds. HRG contains a conserved histidine-rich region that binds cations including divalent nickel, and paired plasma-liver analysis confirmed hepatic-driven synthesis. Blood cell pellet proteomics revealed that Ni-Cr co-exposure predominantly disrupts the nuclear compartment: histone depletion indicated chromatin collapse, NUP153 dysregulation impaired nuclear pore function, and VRK1/TRIP13 upregulation suggested DNA damage response activation coupled with mitotic checkpoint override. Concurrent RNA processing collapse (DDX17, DHX15, RBMX, ALYREF) and changes in telomere-associated proteins (TERF2IP, hnRNPA1 and VRK1) implicated disrupted genome maintenance. These findings identify HRG as a candidate plasma biomarker of Ni-Cr exposure and reveal a coordinated nuclear toxicity signature linking heavy metal contamination to DNA damage and epigenetic disruption in a free-living vertebrate.

papers.title: Programmable amide bond formation using de novo ligases
papers.abstract: Amide bond formation is of central importance in the chemical industry, underpinning the synthesis of small bioactive molecules, macrocycles, peptides and their conjugates. Conventional methods of amide synthesis rely on stoichiometric coupling agents and costly protecting group manipulations. While biocatalysis can alleviate some of these challenges, enzymes typically operate across a narrow range of substrates and their adaptation to new coupling partners requires extensive engineering. Here we show that de novo amide ligases featuring a cysteine catalytic triad can be programmed computationally to operate across diverse substrate classes with high selectivity. We first designed complementary peptide ligases to selectively functionalise either the N-terminus or a single lysine residue of a polypeptide sequence containing 36 competing lysines. Crystal structures of both ligases show excellent agreement with the designs, with structural modelling suggesting that amidation outcompetes hydrolysis because the catalytically competent geometry forms only upon acceptor binding. We then extended our approach to the synthesis of small bioactive molecules by designing stereoselective ligases that mediate a key amide bonding forming step in the synthesis of the preventative HIV therapeutic lenacapavir. These results establish de novo enzyme design as a programmable platform for achieving selective amide bond formations across a wide range of molecular targets.

papers.title: Distinct Roles of ADP and Magnesium in the Structural Remodeling and Higher-Order Assembly of Peroxiredoxin 2
papers.abstract: 2-Cys peroxiredoxins (Prxs) undergo oligomeric transitions linked to peroxidase and chaperone activities, but the contributions of nucleotides and cations to lipid-dependent assembly remain unclear. We examined phosphatidylserine (PS)-induced Prx2 oligomers using biochemical assays and high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM). Both wild-type (WT) and P44A/S76A mutant (MT) Prx2 formed chaperone-active oligomers, although MT assembled more slowly and exhibited a more compact lateral geometry. Mg disassembled both oligomers, whereas ADP alone predominantly disassembled WT. Under combined Mg-ADP conditions, HS-AFM directly captured oligomer disassembly in both proteins, and separate experiments demonstrated higher-molecular-weight (HMW) assembly. WT HMW assemblies exhibited greater heights and stronger Mant-ADP co-elution than MT. Structural predictions suggested altered local Ser76-mediated contacts without major backbone changes. These results distinguish PS-induced functional switching from Mg- and ADP-dependent remodeling and support, without directly proving, a disassembly-reassembly route to HMW formation.

papers.title: Conserved RNA structural elements mediate WDR5 recognition of the long non-coding RNA UMLILO
papers.abstract: The long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), UMLILO (upstream master lncRNA of the inflammatory chemokine locus), regulates the epigenetic programming of innate immune genes. Although its basic mechanism was revealed in cells, the molecular basis by which UMLILO interacts with its partner, WD repeat-containing protein 5 (WDR5), remained unknown. To understand how UMLILO interacts with WDR5, we determined the secondary structure of UMLILO by chemical probing and performed binding assays, uncovering the multivalent nature of their interaction, involving multiple RNA stem-loops. Conservational analysis revealed a stem-loop structurally conserved across mammals. Furthermore, we found that UMLILO engages multiple sites on the surface of WDR5 as revealed by NMR chemical shift perturbation analysis, and that full-length UMLILO increases WDR5 recruitment into in vitro condensates. Our report provides a detailed characterization of the molecular basis of WDR5 recognition by an RNA and establishes a new paradigm for the role of IPLs in enhancing gene expression.

papers.title: Structure-based discovery of new GPR119 ligands from on-demand tera-scale chemical space
papers.abstract: The orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR119 is involved in glucose homeostasis and is considered a promising target for the treatment of diabetes and other metabolic diseases. The recently solved structures of GPR119 in complex with potential endogenous lipid agonists, including oleoylethanolamide (OEA), provide a solid platform for 3D pharmacology analysis and structure-based ligand discovery. Here, we employed the V-SYNTHES2 approach to screen ~3 trillion on-demand compounds from Enamine xREAL chemical space to identify several new chemotypes of GPR119 agonists and antagonists. Structure-guided analog-by-catalog hit expansion of new chemotypes and stereoselective synthesis resulted in a series of full and partial agonists with low-micromolar potencies in functional assays. Cryo-EM structures of active GPR119-Gs complexes bound to three of the hits validated the docking predictions and established further SAR insights into ligand-receptor interactions, enabling the discovery of BRI-17403 and BRI-17409 agonists with EC50 values of 1.6 M and 1.3 M, respectively. These results demonstrate the utility of structure-based screening of tera-scale on-demand chemical spaces in accelerating drug discovery for therapeutically relevant orphan GPCRs.

papers.title: EngA adopts multiple distinct conformational states during ribosome assembly
papers.abstract: Ribosome assembly, a highly coordinated and crucial cellular process, is assisted by various assembly factors, including GTPases. EngA, an essential P-loop GTPase, is involved in late-stage assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The structures of 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GMPPNP, and EngA-bound GDP alone, without 50S subunit, have been reported previously. However, the molecular mechanism of EngA GTP hydrolysis-assisted 50S maturation remains poorly understood, and structures of the 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GDP have yet to be deciphered. We have reported cryo- EM structures of the Mycobacterium smegmatis 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GTP{gamma}S or GDP at 2.8 - 3.5 [A] resolution. Structural analysis revealed that EngA and 50S subunit undergo a coordinated structural rearrangement, and an assembly intermediate is formed in which the stem-loop of H80 makes base-pair interactions with the junction of H89 and H90, forming a unique stem-loop-junction (SLJ) motif. EngA-bound GDP adopts distinctly different conformations in its ribosome-bound and unbound states. In summary, this study proposed a multi-state conformational model for EngA-assisted ribosome assembly.

papers.title: Decoupling Quantification and Identification for Label-Free Top-Down Proteomics Improves Proteome Coverage
papers.abstract: Quantifying proteoforms is essential for understanding biological processes. The most widely used quantification approach in top-down proteomics (TDP) is label-free quantification (LFQ), where quantification and identification compete for acquisition time. We identified missing values, insufficient fragmentation, and undersampling of low-abundance proteoforms as major factors limiting conventional TDP-LFQ workflows. Our proposed workflow decouples quantification and identification through MS1-only quantification followed by targeted data-dependent MS2 identification. The MS1-only acquisition more than doubled the number of mass features quantified reliably and improved quantification precision. Focusing targeted MS2 acquisition on significantly differentially abundant features enables optimization of MS2 parameters and increases identification coverage by 50%. The workflow was validated across different chromatographic conditions, MS acquisition setups, and sample preparation strategies. In Escherichia coli grown on glucose or acetate, the increased depth enabled by this workflow revealed biological insights inaccessible to a previously published bottom-up proteomics dataset. Overall, decoupling quantification and identification improves quantitative depth and proteoform coverage in TDP-LFQ and provides a flexible strategy for high-sensitivity and high-throughput proteoform quantification.

papers.title: Mapping the reactive cysteine landscape of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 protein
papers.abstract: NOD-like receptor pyring-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that drives assembly of an oligomeric inflammasome complex to stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production and pyroptotic cell death. Extensive research has shown that NLRP3 activation is dependent on intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Despite this, the precise targets of ROS in this process remain undefined. In this study, a combination of chemoproteomics, in vitro biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations were used to characterize reactive Cys and how they may impact NLRP3 conformation and activity status. Affinity-captured NLRP3 was subjected to reverse-thiol trapping to reveal a pool of reactive Cys residues that were identified in subsequent chemoproteomic analyses. C150, C196, and C884 were consistently detected with both in vitro and in cellulo experiments. Several NLRP3 mutants were generated; C150A and C196A (NACHT domain) as well as C933A and C941A (LRR domain) reduced IL-1b output in a reconstituted inflammasome assay. Molecular simulation of Cys sulfenylation in the LRR suggests structural alterations that reposition the trLRR loop to destabilize the inactive NLRP3 structure. Structural modelling provided insights for how Cys oxidation of the LRR may impact on NLRP3 structure. Collectively, the results establish a mechanistic understanding for how ROS may promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

papers.title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Radical Dearomatization of Electrophilic Heterocyclic and Non-Heterocyclic Arenes
papers.abstract: Catalytic asymmetric dearomatization provides a powerful strategy for converting readily available aromatic feedstocks into valuable three-dimensional molecular scaffolds. Despite substantial advances over the past several decades, general methods for catalytic asymmetric dearomatization of electrophilic arenes, particularly non-heterocyclic substrates with high aromatic stabilization energies, remain a challenging task. Here, we report the use of a hydrogen atom transfer mechanism for biocatalytic radical dearomatization of electron-deficient arenes. Repurposing and directed evolution of our previously developed P450 halogen atom transferases furnished hydrogen atom transfer dearomatases that catalyze the stereoselective dearomatization of a range of electrophilic arenes, including electron-deficient indoles, pyrroles, and simple benzene derivatives. These evolved biocatalysts facilitated both diastereodivergent and enantiodivergent radical dearomatization, providing access to fused and spirocyclic chiral scaffolds bearing challenging quaternary and/or contiguous stereocenters. Computational and experimental studies revealed that a strategically positioned active-site lysine residue enables enzyme-controlled proton transfer against the intrinsic thermodynamic stereopreference, allowing catalyst-controlled reversal of diastereoselectivity from a common radical intermediate. Importantly, the evolved dearomatases efficiently transformed challenging arene substrates that proved recalcitrant under previously optimized Fe, Mn and Co-based metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer conditions. Collectively, these results establish new-to-nature metalloredox biocatalysis as a powerful strategy for overcoming longstanding challenges in asymmetric radical catalysis.

papers.title: S. pombe Mto1:Mto2 stabilizes γ-tubulin positions within the γ-TuRC
papers.abstract: Microtubules are present in all eukaryotes and are nucleated by multiprotein {gamma}-tubulin ring complexes ({gamma}-TuRCs), ring-shaped structures that contain several copies of the {gamma}-tubulin small complex ({gamma}-TuSC). {gamma}-TuRCs nucleate microtubules via a template-based mechanism in which the positions of {gamma}-tubulins in the {gamma}-TuSCs match the position of {gamma}-tubulin dimers in the microtubule lattice. Although {gamma}-TuSC proteins are highly conserved, other components of the {gamma}-TuRC can vary in different organisms, as can their relative importance. Here, we characterize two different simplified {gamma}-TuRCs from fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, using recombinant purified proteins and negative stain electron microscopy. We show that a nucleation-incompetent {gamma}-TuRC that contains only {gamma}-TuSC proteins plus the microprotein Mzt1 ({gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1) can form rings as efficiently as a large, nucleation-competent complex (MGM) that additionally contains the proteins Mto1 and Mto2. We find that the position of {gamma}-tubulins in {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 are less well defined than in MGM. Comparative modelling using our electron microscopy and crosslinking mass spectrometry data, together with structures of {gamma}-TuRCs from other organisms, suggests that Mto1 and Mto2 form a multimeric outer mantle surrounding the {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 {gamma}-TuRC. This mantle may stabilize positions of {gamma}-tubulins within MGM, explaining the microtubule-nucleating ability of MGM and highlighting the diversity of non-{gamma}-TuSC proteins in modulating {gamma}-TuRC structure and function.

papers.title: PP271, a novel bacteriophage primase-polymerase, enables Primer-Free DNA Amplification
papers.abstract: Primases are essential enzymes that initiate DNA replication by synthesizing de novo primers for replicative DNA polymerases, which ensure accurate genome duplication owing to their high specificity, fidelity, and processivity. PrimPols have emerged as versatile DNA-initiating enzymes that are widely distributed across diverse replication systems, from bacteriophages to humans. In this work, a novel PrimPol enzyme, PP271, encoded by bacteriophage vB-EfaS-271, was characterized. PP271 belongs to the archaeal-eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily and contains the conserved catalytic core, together with a C-terminal PriCT domain. Enzymatic analysis demonstrated that PP271 functions as a bona fide PrimPol, i.e. a DNA primase capable of synthetizing short DNA primers. PP271 priming activity is strongly stimulated by ADP, which serves as the preferred initiating nucleotide. Additionally, PP271 exhibits relaxed specificity for selecting the priming site, compared to other PrimPols with more restricted template preferences. TruePrime amplification technology combines the Thermus thermophilus PrimPol and the highly processive Phi29 DNA polymerase to achieve primer-free DNA amplification. While highly efficient, further improvements in amplification yield, fidelity and product complexity remain possible. Here, we show that DNA primers synthesized by PP271 are efficiently extended by Phi29 DNA polymerase, enabling their coordinated action. Moreover, the short primers generated by PP271 are expected to minimize the contribution of primase-derived errors to the final amplification product while allowing efficient DNA synthesis across a broader range of sequence contexts. Altogether, these findings identify PP271 as a promising alternative for improving primase-dependent DNA amplification.

papers.title: Positive cooperativity enhances coupling of a second G protein to a GPCR dimer
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell surface integral membrane proteins that transduce environmental, hormonal and neurotransmitter molecular signals into intracellular responses. Here we studied a class D1 fungal receptor, Ste2, an obligate dimer that couples two G proteins per dimer and show that coupling of the second G protein has an 18-fold higher affinity than coupling of the first. The molecular mechanism uncovered suggests that coupling of the first G protein to one protomer stabilizes the adjacent protomer in an active conformation with a pre-formed G protein coupling site, thus increasing the affinity for coupling of the second G protein. Protomer-based stabilization of an adjacent protomer in a unique conformational state within a dimer may represent a general mechanism by which oligomerization alters GPCR pharmacology.

papers.title: Bacterial major vault protein homologs form divergent vault structures
papers.abstract: Vaults are large, enigmatic macromolecular protein complexes composed of symmetrically arranged major vault protein (MVP) subunits with a wide variety of proposed functions. While MVP is conserved in most eukaryotes, its prevalence in other domains of life has not been well studied. Furthermore, whether bacterial MVP homologs assemble into vaults remains unknown. Here, we identify and examine a subset of bacterial MVP homologs and report cryoEM structures of an intact vault from Corallococcus praedator and a half-vault from a Deltaproteobacteria bacterium. Both bacterial vault complexes exhibit architectures unlike any other previously characterized vault with barrel/cap symmetries of D35/C13 and C48/C16, respectively. These data demonstrate that bacterial MVP homologs can assemble into vault structures and highlight the structural diversity of vaults across domains of life.

papers.title: Interventional breath analysis reveals oral microbial conversion of 1,2-Propanediol into Propanal and 1-Propanol
papers.abstract: Background: Orally exhaled breath contains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that may reflect local microbial metabolism as well as systemic processes. Consequently, the breath sampling route can influence VOC profiles and complicate biomarker interpretation. Previous studies have shown that 1-propanol is substantially enriched in orally compared with nasally exhaled breath. Objective: To determine whether a controlled oral challenge with 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PD) induces sampling route-dependent changes in breath 1-propanol concentrations. Methods: Ten healthy volunteers received 0.1 mL 1,2-PD diluted in approximately 50 mL water. The solution was used as an oral rinse for approximately 30 s and then expectorated. Matched oral and nasal end-tidal breath samples were collected before administration, immediately afterwards, and at 15-min intervals. Propanal, 1-propanol, acetol, acetone, and isoprene were analysed using gas chromatograph-ion mobility spectrometer (GC-IMS). Results: Oral 1,2-PD exposure produced a rapid and transient increase in exhaled propanal and 1-propanol signals, with the largest responses immediately after administration and at the second post-intervention measurement. In contrast, nasal signals remained comparatively stable. Acetone and isoprene showed no consistent intervention-related changes, regardless of the sampling route. No reproducible increase in acetol was detected, although interpretation was limited by analytical interference. Conclusion: A controlled oral 1,2-PD challenge elicited a route-specific propanal and 1-propanol response, consistent with local microbial metabolism of 1,2-PD within the oral cavity. Both fucose and 1,2-PD have been previously reported in human saliva, including elevated concentrations in selected disease-associated contexts. Bacteria can degrade salivary mucin glycans, releasing sugars including fucose. Together, these observations motivate investigation of a proposed pathway linking mucin-derived fucose to 1,2-PD and subsequent propanal and 1-propanol formation in the human oral cavity.
